entities.summary:
The second cholera pandemic was a global outbreak of the highly infectious and deadly disease, caused by Vibrio cholerae, that affected millions of people across the world from 1829 to 1852. It was first identified in India and quickly spread to other parts of Asia, Europe, and Africa through trade and human migration. This pandemic had a profound impact on the world, resulting in the deaths of an estimated 150,000 to 300,000 people and leading to significant changes in the way cities and communities were designed and managed.

The pandemic began in 1829 in Jessore, Bengal, and quickly spread to other parts of India, including Calcutta. From there, it spread to other parts of Asia, including China and Southeast Asia, and then to Europe and Africa. The pandemic was particularly devastating in cities, where poor sanitation and inadequate water treatment systems allowed the disease to spread quickly. The pandemic also had a significant impact on the social and economic structures of the time, leading to increased awareness of the need for public health measures and the development of new technologies to treat and prevent the disease.

The second cholera pandemic had a lasting impact on the world, leading to significant changes in the way cities and communities were designed and managed. It also led to the development of new technologies, including the use of chlorine to disinfect water and the construction of modern sewers. The pandemic also had a significant impact on the social and economic structures of the time, leading to increased awareness of the need for public health measures and the development of new technologies to treat and prevent the disease.

The second cholera pandemic is often referred to as the 'ghosts of the past' that haunt cities today. It serves as a stark reminder of the devastating consequences of poor sanitation and inadequate public health measures.
